Working Principle 04

Curiosity Keeps You in the Game

The real risk is not being wrong. It is assuming the game has stopped moving.

2 min read
#Curiosity#ContinuousLearning#Growth

Here’s a fascinating truth in sports:

The moment you think you’ve mastered the game is often the moment you start falling behind.

Not because your performance drops.

But because the baseline of excellence keeps moving forward.

That idea has stayed with me.

After many years in industry, I came to UCLA Anderson expecting most of my learning to come from new frameworks and tools.

Instead, some of the most meaningful growth has come from deliberately walking into rooms where I wasn’t the most familiar with the subject.

Over the past two years, I’ve worked alongside medical, law, and public policy students across sustainability initiatives, nonprofit consulting projects, and much more.

What stood out wasn’t just the difference in how people think, but how openly they shared what they knew while remaining equally curious about perspectives outside their own field.

That combination is rare. And powerful.

To push myself further, I also joined cross-campus, cross-disciplinary experiences, marketing and ethics case competitions, and nonprofit consulting projects.

One of the unique things about UCLA is the range of experiences it enables across disciplines.

Months later, those teams are still working together, continuing to learn and take on new challenges.

That, more than anything, has reinforced the value of cross-boundary collaboration.

UCLA legend John Wooden said success is the peace of mind that comes from knowing you gave your absolute best.

That idea is liberating.

It removes the pressure of always needing to have all the answers.

And replaces it with something more valuable: curiosity.

In the long run, the real risk isn’t being wrong. It’s assuming the game stops moving.
